nameStory: The name 'tall coreopsis' is refreshingly straightforward - this member of the coreopsis genus simply towers over its relatives, reaching impressive heights that make it unmistakable in the field. 'Coreopsis' comes from Greek words meaning 'bug-like appearance,' referring to the shape of the seeds, while 'tripteris' means 'three-winged,' describing the leaf structure.
description: Tall coreopsis is a towering wildflower that can reach 4-9 feet in height, making it one of the giants of New England's late summer wildflower display. It produces bright yellow daisy-like flowers with 8 distinctive petals that have deeply notched tips, giving them a fringed appearance. The plant has a sturdy, upright growth habit with multiple branches near the top, creating a candelabra-like flowering display. Despite its impressive size, it maintains an elegant, airy appearance rather than looking bulky or overwhelming.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Unmistakably tall at 4-9 feet high with a strong, sturdy stem that feels smooth and slightly ridged when you run your fingers along it

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like blooms with exactly 8 petals, each petal deeply notched at the tip creating a fringed or ragged edge that feels soft to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive three-part leaves (compound with three leaflets) that are arranged opposite each other on the stem and feel somewhat rough and papery

idTips.label: Branching
idTips.description: Multiple flowering branches emerge from the upper portion of the main stem, creating a candelabra-like crown of yellow flowers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, flattened seeds with tiny wing-like projections that feel papery and light, easily caught by the wind

habitat: Look for tall coreopsis in moist to wet areas like stream banks, pond edges, wet meadows, and roadside ditches with rich, damp soil. In New England, it's most commonly found in disturbed areas with good soil moisture, including the edges of wetlands and low-lying fields. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and often appears in areas that flood occasionally.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as clusters of compound leaves, growing rapidly from the base with the characteristic three-part leaf structure becoming visible early.
seasonality.summer: The plant rockets upward through early summer, reaching full height by mid-summer and beginning to branch at the top in preparation for flowering.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming occurs from late summer through early fall (August-September), when the bright yellow flowers create spectacular displays. Seeds develop and disperse in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems often persist through winter, standing tall and brown with dried seed heads that rattle in the wind, making identification possible even in dormancy.

funFact: Despite being native to much of eastern North America, tall coreopsis is so uncommon in New England that it's been recorded only 16 times in the entire region - making any sighting a genuinely exciting botanical discovery that's worth reporting to local naturalist groups!
confusionNotes: The extreme height immediately separates tall coreopsis from other yellow wildflowers, but it might be confused with tall sunflowers from a distance. However, sunflowers have much larger flower heads with many more petals and simple (not three-part) leaves that feel rougher and more sandpaper-like.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'tall coreopsis,' some botanists and gardeners also know this plant as 'tall tickseed' - both names refer to the same species, with 'tickseed' being the common name for the entire Coreopsis genus due to the seed shape.
compareHints: Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall. The three-part compound leaves also set it apart, as most other coreopsis have simple leaves or different leaf divisions. The combination of extreme height and compound leaves makes this species unmistakable among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
